name: Leptospirosis

veryLikely: Leptospira interrogans (and other pathogenic Leptospira species)
pathogens.why: Leptospira species transmitted via contact with water or soil contaminated by infected animal urine (notably rodents) is the sole cause; the clinical picture of fever with conjunctival suffusion, myalgia, and exposure history in flood-prone or monsoon settings is sufficiently characteristic to justify early empiric treatment.

investigations.test: Leptospira IgM ELISA / MAT (microscopic agglutination test)
investigations.why: Confirms diagnosis serologically; MAT is the reference standard but often only available at referral labs, so treatment should not be delayed pending results.
Assesses for acute kidney injury, a hallmark of severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) with major prognostic significance.
Jaundice with relatively modest transaminase elevation (compared to viral hepatitis) is a classic pattern in leptospirosis.
Screens for thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk, relevant to hemorrhagic complications.
Often elevated due to myositis, supporting the diagnosis and explaining myalgia.

reason: is consistent with leptospirosis, particularly in monsoon/flood settings. This is treatable with antibiotics, and severe disease (Weil's disease: jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage) carries significant mortality if untreated, so empiric therapy should begin promptly on clinical suspicion.

clinicalPearls: Classically biphasic: an acute leptospiremic phase (fever lasting ~3-10 days, organism culturable/PCR-detectable in blood) followed by an immune phase in which symptoms may resolve as antibodies appear and leptospires can be recovered from urine; the two phases are not always distinct, mild cases may lack the second phase, and severe disease can be monophasic and fulminant (p.1442).
Incubation is usually 1-2 weeks but ranges from 2 to 30 days (p.1442).
Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) is a characteristic but non-pathognomonic sign; muscle pain is intense, especially in the calves, back, and abdomen (p.1442).
Headache is intense and frontal or retro-orbital, sometimes with photophobia, resembling dengue (p.1442).
Weil's syndrome denotes the severe triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage (p.1442-1443).

Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (with or without jaundice) is increasingly recognized as an important and widespread presentation; hemoptysis may not become apparent until the patient is intubated (p.1439, 1442).
Jaundice occurs in only ~5-10% of patients, can be deep with an orange skin cast, and is usually NOT associated with fulminant hepatic necrosis (p.1442).

Aseptic meningitis is more common in children than adults; altered mental status in severe disease may reflect leptospiral meningitis, which can occur in anicteric patients lacking other hallmarks (p.1442-1443).
Autoimmune-associated uveitis is a recognized, potentially chronic late sequela (p.1443).
Idea that specific serogroups cause distinct clinical syndromes has been refuted, although some serovars tend to cause more severe disease (p.1442).
Serology lacks sensitivity in the early acute phase (up to day 5) and cannot guide a timely treatment decision; PCR (notably real-time PCR) can confirm diagnosis during the first 5 days (p.1443).
MAT antibodies generally do not reach detectable levels until the second week of illness, and the antibody response may be blunted by early antibiotics (p.1443).
harrison.pathophysiology: Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin, or mucous membranes (especially conjunctival and oral). The highly motile organisms proliferate, cross tissue barriers, and disseminate hematogenously to all organs (leptospiremic phase), evading innate immune mechanisms such as complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis; an exaggerated proinflammatory response correlates with mortality. With the immune phase, antibodies appear and leptospires clear from blood but persist in liver, lung, kidney, heart, and brain. Renal pathology shows acute tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, progressing to interstitial edema and acute tubular necrosis, with dysregulated nephron transporters causing impaired sodium absorption, potassium wasting, and polyuria. Liver histology shows focal (not widespread) hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, bile canaliculus plugging, and hepatocyte apoptosis, with disruption of intercellular junctions and bile leakage. Petechiae and hemorrhages occur across many organs. Hemorrhage is associated with thrombocytopenia (likely platelet consumption); a consumptive coagulopathy with elevated coagulation-activation markers, reduced anticoagulant markers, and dysregulated fibrinolysis may progress to overt DIC. Endothelial cell activation (raised soluble E-selectin and von Willebrand factor) correlates with severity, and leptospires/leptospiral proteins disrupt endothelial barrier function, increasing permeability. The LPS has unusually low endotoxic potency, yet serovar-specific anti-LPS antibodies are central to protective humoral immunity (p.1441-1442).
additionalDifferentials: Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 / other respiratory viral infections (when fever, headache, myalgia predominate)
Hantavirus infection (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome)
Yellow fever and other viral hemorrhagic fevers (Rift Valley fever, filovirus infections, Lassa fever) when bleeding is present
infectionMimics: Dengue (and dengue hemorrhagic fever when bleeding present)
additionalInvestigations: PCR (notably real-time PCR) of blood/CSF/urine - confirms diagnosis with high accuracy during the first 5 days of illness, before serology becomes positive (p.1443)

Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) using live leptospiral strains - paired acute/convalescent sera seeking a fourfold rise; single high titer (1:200-1:800 depending on endemicity) supportive (p.1443)
IgM ELISA and commercial rapid lateral-flow / latex agglutination tests (useful where MAT/culture unavailable) (p.1443)
Blood/urine/CSF culture (special media; may take weeks to months) (p.1441, 1443)
C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR (raised inflammatory markers) (p.1443)
Coagulation profile / DIC markers (D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C) in severe disease (p.1443)
Serum amylase (often elevated even without overt pancreatitis) (p.1443)
Serum electrolytes including magnesium (urinary magnesium loss is characteristic; hypokalemia, hyponatremia) (p.1443)
Urinalysis (leukocytes, erythrocytes, hyaline/granular casts, mild proteinuria) (p.1443)
Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase (bilirubin may be high; transaminase rises typically only moderate) (p.1443)
Chest radiograph / CT (patchy bilateral lower-lobe alveolar pattern from alveolar hemorrhage; pleura-based densities; ground-glass ARDS pattern) (p.1443)
ECG (nonspecific ST/T changes; repolarization abnormalities and arrhythmias are poor prognostic signs) (p.1443)
CSF examination when meningitis suspected (pleocytosis from a few to >1000 cells/uL, lymphocytic but may be PMN-predominant early; protein normal or slightly raised, glucose normal) (p.1443)
Co-testing for rickettsiae, dengue, and hantavirus given overlap and reported dual infections (p.1443)
redFlags: Acute kidney injury / oliguria or anuria
Respiratory insufficiency, hemoptysis, or pulmonary hemorrhage
Cardiac arrhythmias and repolarization abnormalities on ECG
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <=100 x10^9/L) - linked to bleeding and renal failure
harrison.prognosis: Most patients recover, with renal and hepatic function typically returning to normal in survivors (hemodialysis can be lifesaving). Overall mean case-fatality is near 10% for severe cases; severe leptospirosis carries a case-fatality of 1-50%. Mortality is highest in the elderly and those with pulmonary hemorrhage or Weil's syndrome. Untreated leptospiral meningitis has reported mortality of ~13% versus ~2% with antibiotics. Pregnancy is associated with high fetal mortality. Post-leptospirosis sequelae include prolonged fatigue, myalgia, malaise, headache, depression-like symptoms persisting for years, and chronic autoimmune uveitis (p.1443-1444).
pitfalls: Absence of a travel or freshwater-exposure history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1443).
Absence of renal involvement does not rule out leptospirosis (p.1443).
Relying on serology in the first ~5 days risks a false-negative; antibodies are often undetectable until the second week and early antibiotics blunt the response (p.1443).
Cross-reactions are frequent in MAT, so the infecting serovar/serogroup cannot be definitively identified without isolating the organism (p.1443).
Leptospiral meningitis may present without jaundice or other classic severe-disease hallmarks, making it easy to miss (p.1443).
Jaundice can be profound yet usually does not signify fulminant hepatic necrosis, so hepatic transaminase rises are only moderate (p.1442-1443).
The transient rash may be misdiagnosed as scrub typhus or a viral exanthem (p.1442).
Dual infection (e.g., with dengue, rickettsiae, or hantavirus) can occur, so a positive alternative test does not exclude leptospirosis (p.1443).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison distinguishes mild leptospirosis (sudden-onset flu-like febrile illness with headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion; usually self-limiting over 7-10 days, low mortality) from severe leptospirosis, which is often rapidly progressive with multiorgan involvement. Severe disease classically presents as Weil's syndrome (triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage) and/or severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, with a case-fatality of 1-50% (p.1442-1443).
